claim: C. elegans has two sexes: XX hermaphrodites and XO males.
source: C. elegans has two sexes: XX hermaphrodites and XO males.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans biology stated directly in the text.

claim: Hermaphrodites can produce hermaphrodite progeny by self-fertilization.
source: The somatically female hermaphrodites can produce hermaphrodite progeny by self-fertilization (although rare males are generated through spontaneous X chromosome loss)
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans reproduction stated in the text.

claim: Hermaphrodites can mate with males to give rise to equal ratios of hermaphrodites and males.
source: whereas in the presence of males, they are also able to mate with males to give rise to equal ratios of hermaphrodites and males (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans reproduction stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Hermaphrodites from crossing are more sensitive to aldicarb than hermaphrodites from self-fertilization.
source: We found that around 39.8% of hermaphrodites from self-fertilization were paralyzed after 70 min' exposure to aldicarb. In contrast, almost all of the hermaphrodites from crossing were paralyzed (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from aldicarb assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The NMJ E/I ratio is increased in crossed hermaphrodites compared to those obtained by self-fertilization.
source: Thus, the NMJ E/I ratio is increased in crossed hermaphrodites than those obtained by self-fertilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the aldicarb sensitivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hermaphrodites cultured in male-conditioned medium become paralyzed earlier than those in hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: After growing hermaphrodites in the conditioned medium, we found that the hermaphrodites cultured in the male-conditioned medium became paralyzed earlier than those in the hermaphrodite-conditioned medium (80.31% vs. 61.11% paralyzed after 70 min' exposure to aldicarb) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from aldicarb assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The effect of the male environment on hermaphrodite NMJ is mediated by male-secreted metabolites.
source: This result suggests that the effect of the male environment on hermaphrodite NMJ is mediated by male-secreted metabolites.
evidence: This is inferred from the conditioned medium experiments showing that direct contact with males is not required.

claim: The baseline GCaMP3 fluorescence is higher in hermaphrodites grown in male-conditioned medium compared with those grown in hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: We found that the baseline GCaMP3 fluorescence is higher in hermaphrodites grown in the male-conditioned medium compared with those grown in the hermaphrodite-conditioned medium, suggesting relatively higher resting muscle excitability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GCaMP3 fluorescence intensity potentiation is significantly increased in hermaphrodites grown in male-conditioned medium upon optogenetic activation of cholinergic motor neurons.
source: Moreover, we excited the VB and DB cholinergic motor neurons via optogenetic activation of Chrimson with red light (wavelength at 640 nm) (Klapoetke et al., 2014) and observed significantly increased GCaMP3 fluorescence intensity potentiation (assessed as ΔF/F) in hermaphrodites grown in the male-conditioned medium (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic calcium imaging data shown in Figures 1F-G, with citation to the Chrimson method.

claim: The male excretome environment causes increased excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission ratio and muscle excitability at the NMJ of hermaphrodites.
source: These results indicate that the male excretome environment causes increased excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission ratio and muscle excitability at the NMJ of hermaphrodites.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium imaging and aldicarb sensitivity data.

claim: The mEPSC frequency was significantly increased in hermaphrodites from male-conditioned medium compared to those from hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: We found that the mEPSC frequency was significantly increased in hermaphrodites from male-conditioned medium compared to those from hermaphrodite-conditioned medium (Figure 1H,I)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 1H and 1I.

claim: The mEPSC amplitude was not changed between hermaphrodites from male-conditioned and hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: but the mEPSC amplitude was not changed (Figure 1H,J).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 1H and 1J.

claim: No significant differences in mIPSC frequency and amplitude were detected between hermaphrodites from male- or hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: When we examined inhibitory postsynaptic currents, we detected no significant differences in mIPSC frequency and amplitude between hermaphrodites from male- or hermaphrodite-conditioned medium (Figure 1K–M).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 1K-M.

claim: Potentiation of acetylcholine transmission rate mainly contributes to the observed increase in the E/I ratio at the NMJ of hermaphrodites in the male excretome environment.
source: The electrophysiology data suggest that potentiation of acetylcholine transmission rate mainly contributes to the observed increase in the E/I ratio at the NMJ of hermaphrodites in the male excretome environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology data showing increased mEPSC frequency but no change in mIPSC properties.

claim: Exposure to male-conditioned medium at the egg, L1, and L2-L3 stage results in significantly increased sensitivity to aldicarb in young adults.
source: The hermaphrodites transferred to the male-conditioned medium at the egg, L1, and L2–L3 stage presented significantly increased sensitivity to aldicarb when they grow into young adult (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C, 92.5% vs. 55.1% at 70 min for egg stage, 46.9% vs. 24.9% for the L1 stage, and 71.3% vs. 14.0% for L2–L3 stage).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from developmental stage-specific exposure experiments shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figures.

claim: No differences in sensitivity to aldicarb were observed between hermaphrodites transferred to male-conditioned medium at the mid-L4 stage and those from hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: In contrast, we observed no differences in sensitivity to aldicarb between hermaphrodites transferred to male-conditioned medium at the mid-L4 stage and those from hermaphrodite-conditioned medium (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, 15.9% vs. 14.0% at 70 min).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Exposure to the male excretome environment in L3-L4 stage is critical for modulation of the NMJ synaptic transmission in hermaphrodites.
source: Those data suggest that exposure to the male excretome environment in L3–L4 stage is critical for modulation of the NMJ synaptic transmission in hermaphrodites.
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental stage-specific exposure experiments.

claim: Hermaphrodites leaving the male excretome environment at the young adult stage still show increased sensitivity to aldicarb compared with those in the hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: We found that hermaphrodites leaving the male excretome environment at the young adult stage still showed an increased sensitivity to aldicarb compared with those in the hermaphrodite-conditioned medium (66.3% vs. 42.0% at 70 min).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from removal experiments.

claim: The maintenance of the elevated cholinergic synaptic transmission rate at the hermaphrodites NMJ does not require a sustained male excretome environment in adults.
source: suggesting that the maintenance of the elevated cholinergic synaptic transmission rate at the hermaphrodites NMJ does not require a sustained male excretome environment in adults.
evidence: This is inferred from the removal experiments showing persistent effects after removal from male environment.

claim: The male-conditioned medium accelerated animal paralysis in the CB4856 strain.
source: We observed that the male-conditioned medium accelerated animal paralysis in the CB4856 (Figure 2D, 59.7% vs. 20.7% after 60 min of aldicarb)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the CB4856 strain shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The male-conditioned medium accelerated animal paralysis in the AB3 strain.
source: and the AB3 strains (Figure 2E, 52.8% vs. 28.6% after 80 min of aldicarb)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the AB3 strain shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The male-conditioned medium did not accelerate animal paralysis in the TR389 strain.
source: but not in the TR389 strain (Figure 2F, 68.46% vs. 60.99% after 130 min of aldicarb).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the TR389 strain shown in Figure 2F.

claim: TR389 males appear unable to secrete the modulator ascarosides.
source: Thus, TR389 males appear unable to secrete the modulator ascarosides.
evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing N2 hermaphrodites do not respond to TR389 male-conditioned medium but TR389 hermaphrodites respond to N2 male-conditioned medium.

claim: Males have higher body curvature and locomotor velocity than hermaphrodites.
source: We observed that males had higher body curvature and locomotor velocity than hermaphrodites (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B), consistent with previous studies (Mowrey et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B and cited previous work.

claim: The locomotor velocities of hermaphrodites from male-conditioned medium are significantly lower than those from hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: However, the locomotor velocities of hermaphrodites from male-conditioned medium are significantly lower than those from hermaphrodite-conditioned medium (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion analysis data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: No significant differences in brood size were observed between hermaphrodites from hermaphrodite- and male-conditioned medium.
source: We calculated the brood size of hermaphrodites from hermaphrodite- and male-conditioned medium, and observed no significant differences between the two groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by egg-laying behavior data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Hermaphrodites from N2 male-conditioned medium have higher mating efficiency than those from hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: we found that N2 male-conditioned medium showed a significant further increase of hermaphrodite mating efficiency than the TR389 male-conditioned medium (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by mating efficiency data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Ascarosides function as pheromones to mediate social interactions in C. elegans.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans), a family of glycolipids called ascarosides function as the pheromones to mediate social interactions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans pheromones stated in the text.

claim: Males and hermaphrodites secrete several ascarosides in different amounts that elicit sexual dimorphic responses.
source: Males and hermaphrodites secrete several ascarosides in different amounts that elicit sexual dimorphic responses (Butcher et al., 2007; Edison, 2009; Greene et al., 2016; Srinivasan et al., 2008; Srinivasan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work on ascarosides.

claim: The male-enriched ascr#10 induces attraction behavior in hermaphrodites but causes aversion behavior in males.
source: For example, the male-enriched ascr#10 induces attraction behavior in hermaphrodites, but causes aversion behavior in males (Izrayelit et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on ascr#10.

claim: DAF-22 β-oxidizes and shortens long-chain fatty acids to generate bioactive medium- and short-chain ascarosides.
source: Ascarosides are derivatives of 3,6-dideoxysugar ascarylose, and their biosynthesis requires several dehydrogenases, including DAF-22, which β-oxidizes and shortens long-chain fatty acids to generate bioactive medium- and short-chain ascarosides (Figure 3A; Butcher et al., 2009; von Reuss et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on ascaroside biosynthesis and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Most of the active short- and medium-chain ascarosides are absent from the metabolomes of daf-22 mutants.
source: Therefore, most of the active short- and medium-chain ascarosides are absent from the metabolomes of daf-22 mutants (Butcher et al., 2009; von Reuss et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on daf-22 mutants.

claim: Hermaphrodites grown in daf-22 male-conditioned medium exhibited similar aldicarb sensitivity with those grown in daf-22 hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: We found that the hermaphrodites grown in the daf-22 male-conditioned medium exhibited similar aldicarb sensitivity with those grown in daf-22 hermaphrodite-conditioned medium (Figure 3B, 43.7% vs. 43.7% at 70 min).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Male-specific ascarosides contribute to the observed modulatory effects on synaptic transmission.
source: The inability of the daf-22 male environment to modulate hermaphrodite NMJ synaptic transmission suggests that male-specific ascarosides do contribute to the observed modulatory effects on synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the daf-22 mutant experiments.

claim: Males from hermaphrodite- and male-conditioned medium did not show differences in aldicarb sensitivity.
source: To study whether the male-specific ascarosides also modulate male NMJ synaptic transmission, we compared the aldicarb sensitivity of males grown in the hermaphrodite- and male-conditioned media. We did not observe aldicarb sensitivity differences in males from hermaphrodite- and male-conditioned medium (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: daf-22 males from male-conditioned medium did not show significant differences in aldicarb sensitivity compared to those from hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: We also found that daf-22 males from the male-conditioned medium did not show any significant differences in aldicarb sensitivity compared to those from the hermaphrodite-conditioned medium (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Male-specific ascarosides cannot modulate synaptic transmission in males, suggesting a sexually dimorphic effect.
source: These results indicate that male-specific ascarosides cannot modulate synaptic transmission in males, suggesting a sexually dimorphic effect of those male-specific ascarosides.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing no effect of male pheromones on male synaptic transmission.

claim: Medium-chain β-hydroxylated ascarosides were substantially increased in N2 male cultures compared to N2 hermaphrodite cultures and TR389 male cultures.
source: The medium-chain β-hydroxylated ascarosides were substantially increased in the N2 male cultures compared to the N2 hermaphrodite cultures and TR389 male cultures. Specifically, the significantly enriched β-hydroxylated ascarosides in N2 males included C13, C14, and C15 ascarosides (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by UPLC-MS data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: No significant changes were detected between N2 and TR389 male cultures for saturated ascarosides.
source: Notably, we detected no significant changes between the N2 and TR389 male cultures for saturated ascarosides (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by UPLC-MS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Medium-chain β-hydroxylated ascarosides may act as the male modulator ascarosides.
source: These results implicate that the medium-chain β-hydroxylated ascarosides may act as the male modulator ascarosides.
evidence: This is inferred from the UPLC-MS analysis comparing different strains and conditions.

claim: dhs-28 mutant hermaphrodites were more sensitive to aldicarb compared with N2 hermaphrodites.
source: As expected, dhs-28 mutant hermaphrodites were more sensitive to aldicarb compared with N2 hermaphrodites (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: dhs-28 hermaphrodites cannot be modulated by male ascarosides.
source: Furthermore, we examined the male ascaroside effects on dhs-28 mutants, which could accumulate β-hydroxylated medium-chain ascarosides themselves. The result showed that dhs-28 hermaphrodites cannot be modulated by male ascarosides by presenting comparable aldicarb sensitivity when in hermaphrodite- and male-conditioned medium (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Environmental enrichment of β-hydroxylated medium-chain ascarosides increases the hermaphrodite NMJ E/I ratio.
source: These experiments with ascaroside biosynthesis mutants establish that environmental enrichment of β-hydroxylated medium-chain ascarosides increases the hermaphrodite NMJ E/I ratio, thereby supporting that these specific ascarosides may function as NMJ cholinergic synaptic transmission modulators.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic experiments with ascaroside biosynthesis mutants.

claim: Ablation of the AWB neuron pair in hermaphrodites blocked the increased sensitivity to aldicarb following exposure to male-conditioned medium.
source: Ablation of the AWB (str-1 promoter driving miniSOG) neuron pair in hermaphrodites blocked the increased sensitivity to aldicarb following exposure to the male-conditioned medium (Figure 4B,C, 45.6% vs. 43.4% at 80 min).
evidence: This is supported by genetic ablation experiments shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: The increased aldicarb sensitivity in the male-conditioned medium remained when any other chemosensory neurons were ablated.
source: In contrast, the increased aldicarb sensitivity in the male-conditioned medium remained when any other chemosensory neurons were ablated (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–G).
evidence: This is supported by genetic ablation experiments shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: Ablation of AWB neurons blocked the decreased velocity by the modulator ascarosides.
source: In addition, ablation of AWB neurons blocked the decreased velocity by the modulator ascarosides (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion analysis data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: AWB neurons in hermaphrodites are necessary for the effects of male-specific modulator ascarosides on NMJ synaptic transmission.
source: These results support that AWB neurons in hermaphrodites are necessary for the effects of male-specific modulator ascarosides on NMJ synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the AWB ablation experiments.

claim: Hermaphrodites with activated AWB neurons during the L4 stage showed higher sensitivity to aldicarb than controls without blue light activation.
source: Nevertheless, hermaphrodites with activated AWB neurons during the L4 stage showed higher sensitivity to aldicarb than controls without blue light activation (ATR+ light+ vs. ATR+ light−) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic activation experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Activation of the AWB chemosensory neuron pair in hermaphrodites is sufficient to modulate the NMJ synaptic transmission.
source: These findings confirm that activation of the AWB chemosensory neuron pair in hermaphrodites is sufficient to modulate the NMJ synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: AWB neurons elicited a rapid and robust calcium transient responding to male excretomes.
source: We found that the AWB neurons elicited a rapid and robust calcium transient responding to the male excretomes.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: No responses were detected in AWB neurons by stimulation with hermaphrodite excretomes.
source: However, no responses were detected by stimulation with the hermaphrodite excretomes (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 4F-H.

claim: AWB neurons directly respond to the male-specific modulator ascarosides.
source: Collectively, the data support that AWB neurons directly respond to the male-specific modulator ascarosides.
evidence: This is inferred from the calcium imaging experiments showing AWB responses to male excretomes.

claim: No differences in sensitivity to aldicarb were observed for tax-2 mutant hermaphrodites upon exposure to male-conditioned or hermaphrodite-conditioned media.
source: We observed no differences in sensitivity to aldicarb for tax-2 mutant hermaphrodites upon exposure to the male-conditioned or hermaphrodite-conditioned media (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Complementing TAX-2 expression in AWB neurons rescued the increased aldicarb sensitivity phenotype of hermaphrodites grown in male-conditioned medium.
source: Further supporting this, complementing TAX-2 expression in AWB neurons rescued the increased aldicarb sensitivity phenotype of hermaphrodites grown in the male-conditioned medium (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The increased sensitivity to aldicarb was rescued by ODR-3 complementation in AWB neurons.
source: The increased sensitivity to aldicarb was also rescued by ODR-3 complementation in AWB neurons (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The cGMP signaling pathway in AWB chemosensory neurons transmits male-specific modulator ascaroside signals to the NMJ.
source: Together, these results establish that the cGMP signaling pathway in AWB chemosensory neurons transmits male-specific modulator ascaroside signals to the NMJ.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic experiments with tax-2 and odr-3 mutants and rescue experiments.

claim: Puncta fluorescence intensities and densities of RAB-3-GFP at cholinergic synapses were comparable in hermaphrodites grown in either hermaphrodite- or male-conditioned medium.
source: We observed that puncta fluorescence intensities and densities were comparable in hermaphrodites grown in either hermaphrodite- or male-conditioned medium (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The excitatory synapse structures were unaltered by the presence of modulator ascarosides.
source: which suggested that the excitatory synapse structures were unaltered by the presence of modulator ascarosides.
evidence: This is inferred from the RAB-3-GFP imaging data.

claim: The puncta fluorescence intensities and densities in the inhibitory GABAergic synapses did not differ between hermaphrodites from male-conditioned or hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: Similar to the excitatory cholinergic synapses, the puncta fluorescence intensities and densities in the inhibitory GABAergic synapses did not differ between hermaphrodites from male-conditioned or hermaphrodite-conditioned medium (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Neither excitatory nor inhibitory synapse structures are affected by the modulator ascarosides.
source: which collectively suggest that neither excitatory nor inhibitory synapse structures are affected by the modulator ascarosides.
evidence: This is inferred from the RAB-3 imaging data for both cholinergic and GABAergic synapses.

claim: Hermaphrodites from male-conditioned medium had a slight but significant increase in puncta signal intensities for nAchRs at cholinergic synapses compared to those from hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: At cholinergic synapses, the hermaphrodites from the male-conditioned medium had a slight but significant increase in puncta signal intensities for the nAchRs compared to those from the hermaphrodite-conditioned medium (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data of ACR-16-RFP and UNC-29-RFP shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: GABAAR intensities were not changed between hermaphrodites from male-conditioned and hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: However, the GABAAR intensities were not changed (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data of UNC-49-mCherry shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Both the nAchRs and GABAAR densities were unaltered between hermaphrodites from male-conditioned and hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: Both the nAchRs and GABAAR densities were unaltered (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 5C-E.

claim: The male-specific modulator ascarosides are involved in increased postsynaptic receptor abundance at excitatory synapses in hermaphrodites.
source: Thus, the male-specific modulator ascarosides are involved in increased postsynaptic receptor abundance at excitatory synapses in hermaphrodites.
evidence: This is inferred from the receptor imaging data showing increased nAchR intensities.

claim: N-type voltage-gated calcium channels (CaV2) are required for the presynaptic calcium influx process that underlies both excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission.
source: N-type voltage-gated calcium channels (CaV2) are required for the presynaptic calcium influx process that underlies both excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission (Liu et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on CaV2 channels.

claim: CaV2-splitGFP is localized correctly at presynaptic elements.
source: The CaV2-GFP fusion protein formed fluorescent puncta largely co-localized with UNC-57/Endophilin in dorsal cord axons (Figure 6B,C, Pearson correlation coefficient 0.7808 ± 0.022 for DA/DB cholinergic motor terminals, and 0.7880 ± 0.0175 for GABAergic motor neuron terminals), confirming that CaV2-splitGFP is localized correctly at presynaptic elements.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization imaging data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: UNC-57/endophilin fluorescence intensities and densities were indistinguishable in hermaphrodites from hermaphrodite- and male-conditioned medium.
source: We further found that UNC-57/endophilin fluorescence intensities and densities were indistinguishable in hermaphrodites from the hermaphrodite- and male-conditioned medium (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presynaptic structure is not altered by male pheromone.
source: This result is consistent with RAB-3-GFP imaging results and support that the presynaptic structure is not altered by male pheromone (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is inferred from the UNC-57 imaging data and RAB-3 imaging data.

claim: CaV2 puncta fluorescence intensities were significantly increased at cholinergic synapses of hermaphrodites from male-conditioned medium compared to those from hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: Comparison of the CaV2 puncta fluorescence intensities revealed a significant increase at cholinergic synapses of hermaphrodites from male-conditioned medium compared to those from the hermaphrodite-conditioned medium (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by CaV2-splitGFP imaging data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A slight but notable increase in CaV2 densities was observed at cholinergic synapses of hermaphrodites from male-conditioned medium.
source: A slight but notable increase in densities was also observed (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by CaV2-splitGFP imaging data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: No significant differences in CaV2 puncta fluorescence intensities and densities were detected at GABAergic synapses between hermaphrodites from male-conditioned and hermaphrodite-conditioned medium.
source: In contrast, we detected no significant differences in CaV2 puncta fluorescence intensities and densities at GABAergic synapses (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by CaV2-splitGFP imaging data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The mEPSC rate in unc-2 mutant was decreased compared to wild type.
source: The mEPSC rate and locomotion velocity in the unc-2 mutant were decreased compared to those in the wild type (Figure 7A,B)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: The male-specific ascarosides no longer increase mEPSC rates in unc-2 hermaphrodites.
source: Furthermore, we found that the male-specific ascarosides no longer increase mEPSC rates in the unc-2 hermaphrodites (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 7A-C.

claim: The locomotion velocity was not changed in unc-2 hermaphrodites from male-condition medium compared to those from hermaphrodite-condition medium.
source: Similarly, the locomotion velocity was not changed in unc-2 hermaphrodites from male-condition medium compared to those from hermaphrodite-condition medium (Figure 7D)
evidence: This is supported by locomotion analysis data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: unc-2 mutation blocks the effects of the male-specific modulator ascarosides on NMJ synaptic transmission.
source: which suggests that unc-2 mutation blocks the effects of the male-specific modulator ascarosides on NMJ synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the unc-2 mutant experiments showing no response to male pheromones.

claim: The male-specific modulator ascarosides may promote the accumulation of CaV2 calcium channels at excitatory cholinergic synapses, accounting for the potentiated cholinergic synaptic transmission at NMJ.
source: These findings collectively indicate that the male-specific modulator ascarosides may promote the accumulation of CaV2 calcium channels at excitatory cholinergic synapses, accounting for the potentiated cholinergic synaptic transmission at NMJ.
evidence: This is inferred from the CaV2 imaging data and unc-2 mutant experiments.

claim: The male environment modulates the NMJ synaptic transmission, locomotion behavior, and mating efficiency in hermaphrodites.
source: In this study, we have revealed a novel mechanism through which the male environment modulates the NMJ synaptic transmission, locomotion behavior, and mating efficiency in hermaphrodites.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.

claim: The male environment effects are mediated based on exposure to male-specific pheromones at a specific developmental stage in hermaphrodites (the entire L3-L4 stage).
source: We show that the male environment effects are mediated based on exposure to male-specific pheromones at a specific developmental stage in hermaphrodites (the entire L3–L4 stage).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the developmental timing findings.

claim: Hermaphrodite sense and process male-specific pheromones by AWB chemosensory neurons using the cGMP signaling.
source: We further demonstrate that hermaphrodite sense and process these male-specific pheromones by AWB chemosensory neurons using the cGMP signaling.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the circuit findings.

claim: Presynaptic calcium channel localization and postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor clustering are elevated by exposure to male-specific pheromones at the hermaphrodite NMJ.
source: At the hermaphrodite NMJ, presynaptic calcium channel localization and postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor clustering are elevated by exposure to male-specific pheromones, resulting in an increased cholinergic synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the synaptic mechanism findings.

claim: The C. elegans NMJ is a useful model to study synaptic transmission in vivo.
source: Here, we used the C. elegans NMJ as a model to study synaptic transmission, and our work underscore C. elegans as a useful model to study synaptic transmission in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the model system used in the study.

claim: Mechanisms of synaptogenesis and synaptic transmission are shared by the C. elegans NMJ and the mammalian central nervous system.
source: Both our and others' studies have identified mechanisms of synaptogenesis and synaptic transmission that are shared by the C. elegans NMJ and the mammalian central nervous system (Dolphin and Lee, 2020; Hata et al., 1993; Ogawa et al., 1998; Pevsner et al., 1994; Richmond et al., 1999; Rizo and Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work showing conservation of mechanisms.

claim: Many autism-linked synaptic proteins have conserved roles in NMJ synaptogenesis and synaptic transmission.
source: It is also highly notable that many autism-linked synaptic proteins, including Neuroligins and Neurexins, have been shown to function with conserved roles in NMJ synaptogenesis and synaptic transmission (Hart and Hobert, 2018; Hu et al., 2012; Kurshan et al., 2018; Philbrook et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on autism-linked proteins in C. elegans.

claim: The mechanisms identified in the C. elegans NMJ may provide new insights into how synaptic transmission is maintained in the mammalian brain.
source: Thus, the mechanisms we identified here in the C. elegans NMJ may provide new insights into how synaptic transmission is maintained in the mammalian brain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: A previously unknown circuit comprised of AWB chemosensory neurons regulates NMJ synaptic transmission in C. elegans.
